title: DevOps & SRE
summary: Shipping software and keeping it running. Two thresholds change how the work is seen: infrastructure as code (servers are text you review and version), and the error budget (reliability is a target you spend, not a perfection you chase).
sources: Kim, Humble, Debois, Willis: The DevOps Handbook
Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy: Site Reliability Engineering (Google)

nodes.label: Linux & Processes
nodes.summary: Processes, signals, permissions, services and logs: the operating system every server runs.
nodes.outcome: Find and stop a runaway process and read its service logs.
nodes.check: A service won't start. Which two commands show its status and recent logs under systemd?

nodes.label: Networking for Operators
nodes.summary: DNS, ports, TLS, load balancers and firewalls: how a request reaches a service.
nodes.outcome: Trace a failing request from DNS to the service port.
nodes.check: `curl https://api.example.com` fails but `curl https://10.0.0.5` works. What is the likely fault?
nodes.answer: DNS: the name does not resolve to that address.

nodes.label: Containers & Images
nodes.summary: A process isolated with namespaces and cgroups, started from an immutable layered image.
nodes.outcome: Write a Dockerfile and explain each layer's cache behaviour.
nodes.check: Why copy dependency manifests and install them before copying the source code in a Dockerfile?
nodes.answer: Layers are cached: dependencies change rarely, so code edits don't force a reinstall.

nodes.label: "A container is a lightweight VM"
nodes.summary: Containers share the host kernel; they are isolated processes, not machines. That changes security and what can run inside them.
nodes.outcome: Explain what a container shares with its host.
nodes.check: Can a Linux container run a Windows kernel driver on a Linux host?
nodes.answer: No: containers share the host's kernel; there is no separate guest kernel.

nodes.label: Continuous Integration
nodes.summary: Every change is merged often and verified by an automated build and test run.
nodes.outcome: Write a CI pipeline that builds, tests and fails fast.
nodes.check: What does 'integrate continuously' actually require of developers?
nodes.answer: Merging small changes to the main line at least daily, each verified by the automated build and tests.

nodes.label: Continuous Delivery & Deployment
nodes.summary: Every passing build is releasable; deployment strategies (blue-green, canary, rolling) limit the blast radius.
nodes.outcome: Choose a deployment strategy for a risky change and plan its rollback.
nodes.check: What does a canary release do?
nodes.answer: Sends a small share of traffic to the new version first, and widens it only if metrics stay healthy.

nodes.label: Infrastructure as Code
nodes.summary: Servers, networks and permissions declared as reviewed, versioned text and applied by tools. Troublesome because 'just fix it on the box' becomes drift.
nodes.outcome: Declare an environment in code and reproduce it from scratch.
nodes.check: Someone hot-fixes a server by hand. Why is that a problem under infrastructure as code?
nodes.answer: The server drifts from its declared state: the next apply may undo the fix, and nobody can reproduce it.

nodes.label: "Servers should be fixed by hand when they break"
nodes.summary: Treating servers as pets to nurse back to health, instead of cattle to replace from code.
nodes.outcome: Replace, rather than repair, a broken instance from its definition.
nodes.check: A server's disk is corrupted. Under 'cattle, not pets', what do you do?
nodes.answer: Destroy it and recreate it from code and images, then investigate from logs and metrics.

nodes.label: Configuration & Secrets
nodes.summary: Config in the environment, not the code; secrets in a vault with rotation and least privilege.
nodes.outcome: Move a hard-coded secret to a secret store and rotate it.
nodes.check: An API key was committed to git and then deleted in the next commit. Is it safe?
nodes.answer: No: it is still in history. Rotate the key immediately.

nodes.label: Orchestration (Kubernetes)
nodes.summary: Desired state reconciled continuously: pods, deployments, services, health probes and autoscaling.
nodes.outcome: Deploy a service with readiness and liveness probes.
nodes.check: What is the difference between a readiness probe and a liveness probe?
nodes.answer: Readiness decides whether to send traffic; liveness decides whether to restart the container.

nodes.label: Observability: Metrics, Logs, Traces
nodes.summary: Instrument services so you can ask new questions of production: the RED and USE methods, structured logs, distributed traces.
nodes.outcome: Instrument a service with RED metrics and find a slow dependency with a trace.
nodes.check: What do the RED metrics stand for?
nodes.answer: Rate, Errors and Duration of requests.

nodes.label: "Average latency tells you how users feel"
nodes.summary: Averages hide the tail. Users notice the p99, and one slow call in a fan-out makes the whole request slow.
nodes.outcome: Read latency percentiles and explain tail amplification.
nodes.check: Mean latency is 50 ms but p99 is 2 s. What does that mean for users?
nodes.answer: 1 in 100 requests takes 2 s or more; for pages making many calls, most users hit at least one slow one.

nodes.label: SLOs & Error Budgets
nodes.summary: Pick a reliability target users actually need; the shortfall from 100% is a budget to spend on change. Troublesome because more reliability is not always better.
nodes.outcome: Set an SLO, compute its error budget and use it to decide on a release freeze.
nodes.check: A 99.9% monthly availability SLO allows how much downtime in a 30-day month?

nodes.label: "The target should be 100% uptime"
nodes.summary: 100% is unreachable and freezes change; users can't tell 99.99% from 100% through their own networks.
nodes.outcome: Argue for an SLO below 100% with the cost of each extra nine.
nodes.check: Why do SRE teams avoid a 100% availability target?
nodes.answer: It is impossible, each extra nine costs far more, and it leaves no budget for releases or experiments.

nodes.label: Incident Response & Postmortems
nodes.summary: Roles (incident commander, comms), mitigation before root cause, and blameless postmortems that change the system.
nodes.outcome: Run an incident: mitigate, communicate, then write a blameless postmortem with actions.
nodes.check: During an outage, what comes first: finding the root cause or mitigating?
nodes.answer: Mitigating (roll back, fail over, shed load); root cause comes after users are safe.

nodes.label: Supply Chain & DevSecOps
nodes.summary: Dependency scanning, signed artifacts, SBOMs and least-privilege pipelines.
nodes.outcome: Add dependency scanning and artifact signing to a pipeline.
nodes.check: Why should a CI pipeline's credentials have the least privilege possible?
nodes.answer: The pipeline runs untrusted code (dependencies, PRs); a compromised job inherits whatever the credentials allow.

nodes.label: Delivery Metrics (DORA)
nodes.summary: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore: speed and stability measured together.
nodes.outcome: Measure the four DORA metrics for a team and pick one to improve.
nodes.check: Accelerate found that speed and stability trade off against each other. True or false?
nodes.answer: False: high performers are better at both.
